extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys/agents, and in-house counsel involved in filing and prosecuting patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing, filing, prosecuting and responding to office actions for patent applications across national, regional (EPO) and PCT systems, including procedural, substantive and cost-related considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive examination: patentability and sufficiency of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Checks whether the application satisfies the patentability criteria and whether the invention is sufficiently disclosed, clearly and completely, in the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During substantive examination the office will give the applicant an opportunity to remove objections (typically by amending). The examiner will compare prior art and the application; if patentability criteria are not met or disclosure is insufficient, office action will be issued. Be prepared to rebut or amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility for fee reductions (national and PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions offer reductions in fees for applications filed by certain parties such as sole inventors, universities, research institutions and/or small companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the United States provides for a 50 percent discount for most fees paid by sole inventors, nonprofits (including universities) and small companies. The PCT offers reductions too (e.g., 90% reduction for certain natural persons and least-developed countries); some ISAs reduce search fees for nationals/residents of certain countries. The patent drafter should investigate and claim small-entity or other status where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-drafter duty to advise on costs and fee strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter should provide sound advice about the costs of patent protection worldwide and offer ideas of how the client might limit its costs by filing only in countries where protection is business-critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise clients about cumulative government and professional fees, translation costs, validation fees, and strategies such as limiting designated countries, using PCT to postpone costs, or relying on international instruments (e.g., London Agreement) to reduce translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and plan for translation requirements and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: To file a patent application in a patent office abroad, the client may need to prepare a translation of the local application into the language accepted by that office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations of complicated legal/technical documents can be very costly; e.g., filing in five further countries requiring five different languages is significant. EPO accepts English, French or German for prosecution but may require translations for validation. Inform clients about instruments like the London Agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the phases of patent grant and associated fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The fees that may be associated with the steps taken include filing fees, publication fees, request for examination fees, search fees, prosecution-related fees, issue fees and maintenance fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all offices require every fee; some require other fees. Each fee may have an associated professional service cost (often higher than government fees). Special procedures (accelerated examination, time-limit extensions) may carry additional fees. Most jurisdictions charge issue and maintenance fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PCT to postpone national phase costs and gain time
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing under the PCT may be a good option from a costs perspective because it postpones major costs and gives additional time to decide on national filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the PCT the applicant typically has at least 30 months from initial filing to begin national phase (vs 12 months under Paris Convention), effectively gaining 18 months to assess patentability and commercial prospects and to postpone translation and national fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT does not create an international patent; national offices decide
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO does not issue a 'PCT patent' or 'international patent' that provides protection in all Contracting States; each national or regional office can grant or reject the patent under its own patent law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must still prosecute in each country/region where protection is sought and pay national/regional fees and comply with local requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory contents of a nonprovisional/utility application (US) and PCT application
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States, a nonprovisional patent application must include claims, an abstract, a description, an oath or declaration and, in most cases, drawings. A PCT international application must contain: a request; a description; one or more claims; one or more drawings, where drawings are necessary; and an abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A provisional application need not include claims. A utility application is the application that includes claims. Ensure required parts are present and in an acceptable language (or accompanied by translation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmittal and fee transmittal forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility patent application transmittal form (or transmittal letter) should be filed with every patent application to inform the office what types of paper are being filed. A fee transmittal form may be used to calculate prescribed filing fees and indicate method of payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transmittal lists contents (description, claims, drawings, declaration, information disclosure statement). Fee transmittal indicates payment method (check, credit card, electronic). Amount payable depends on number/type of claims and small entity status assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment and timing of filing, search and examination fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing, searching and examination fees for a patent application should be paid at the same time as the application is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filed without required fees, the applicant will be notified and asked to submit fees within a given time period; a surcharge may be added for late acceptance. In many jurisdictions request-for-examination fees and other fees apply only in offices that use a request-for-examination system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small entity / written assertion to reduce fees (US example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount payable may be dependent upon whether the client can provide a written assertion of small entity status, such as for individual inventors, which will typically reduce the government fees by half.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure correct small-entity or micro-entity status assertions to obtain fee reductions and maintain records to justify status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application data sheet contents
rubrics_metrics.description: An application data sheet will contain bibliographic data, such as applicant, correspondence, application, representative, domestic priority, foreign priority and assignment information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete and accurate bibliographic data facilitates prosecution and proper assignment/representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath or declaration requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent application should include an oath or declaration signed by the inventor(s) to affirm that they believe themselves to be the original inventor(s) of the subject matter of the application. The oath or declaration must be in a language that the inventor understands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the oath/declaration is in a language other than the required office language (e.g., English for USPTO), an English translation and a statement that the translation is accurate will be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO: designation, validation, translations and opposition trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Because applications filed with the EPO are regional, they must include some indication of the Contracting States desired. Once granted, the applicant must validate the European patent in each Contracting State where protection is sought, typically involving payment of validation fees and submission of documents and translations. Publication of the European patent triggers the time limit for filing an opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO charges a single designation fee regardless of how many countries are designated; after grant validation fees and translations may be required for each national office. Consider designation strategy and translation/validation costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: International search report (ISR) and written opinion as decision tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The international search results in an ISR – a list of published documents that might affect patentability – and a preliminary and nonbinding written opinion on whether the invention appears to meet patentability criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may withdraw, amend claims, or proceed based on ISR and written opinion. ISR and opinion give high-quality insight into likely patentability and can inform national phase decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional supplementary international search (SIS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may request a supplementary international search (SIS) by a SISA, focusing for example on documents in a particular language. A SIS request must be made within 22 months of the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goal is to reduce likelihood of relevant prior art arising later in national phase that could jeopardize grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional international preliminary examination (IPER/IPRP Chapter I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may request an international preliminary examination to amend the international application (e.g., to overcome prior art) and obtain another opinion on patentability 'as amended'; result is an international preliminary examination report (IPER/IPRP Chapter I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If requested, the preliminary examination fee is paid to the IPEA. The IPER provides a stronger basis for evaluating chances of obtaining patents in national phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: National phase entry requirements and time limits
rubrics_metrics.description: After the international phase, the applicant must decide to pursue protection before specific national/regional offices and choose designated offices in which to continue processing before expiry of the time limit, typically 30 months from filing (or priority) date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National phase requirements include payment of national fees and translations of the application if necessary. Failure to meet time limits results in loss of national effect in those states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant/residency/nationality filing requirements under the PCT
rubrics_metrics.description: Any national or resident of one of the PCT Contracting States may file an international patent application. Where there are two or more applicants, at least one must be a national or resident of a Contracting State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In principle, an international application may be filed with the applicant's national office or WIPO. Nationals/residents of regional patent organization members may file with the regional office if permitted. National security provisions may require national filing or authorization before filing abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language acceptability for PCT filing and ISA
rubrics_metrics.description: An international patent application may be filed in any language the receiving office accepts. At least one language should also be acceptable to the ISA and be a PCT publication language; otherwise a translation must be supplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT publication languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish. Plan filings to minimize translation burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT and national phase fee categories and payment timing
rubrics_metrics.description: During the international phase an applicant may pay transmittal, search and international filing fees; if opting for IPER, preliminary examination fee must be paid. In the national phase applicants pay national fees, translation fees and professional fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The receiving office collects some fees, WIPO collects others. National fees must be paid in local currencies and within listed time limits; any due annuities/renewal fees on the international patent must be paid on entry where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT fee reductions and electronic filing discounts
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT offers special reductions of fees for certain applicants (e.g., 90% reduction on certain fees for natural persons from certain countries and least-developed countries). PCT fee reductions are also available to applicants who file electronically, based on filing type and format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some ISAs provide reductions of the international search fee for nationals/residents of certain countries. Check the PCT Applicant’s Guide for details and eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional tip: use PCT Applicant’s Guide and monitoring tools
rubrics_metrics.description: You can find complete information about filing a PCT application, including procedures, timelines and fees, at www.wipo.int/pct and the PCT Applicant’s Guide (updated frequently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sign up to the PCT Newsletter to stay current. Consult national chapters of the PCT Applicant’s Guide for exact national fee amounts and time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent prosecution: advocate skillfully and be proactive
rubrics_metrics.description: In countries requiring substantive examination, a patent drafter must skillfully and articulately advocate the patentability of the client’s invention before the patent office and prepare respectful, complete responses to office actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent drafter should not be passive; be ready to rebut misunderstandings, point to additional information/evidence, and advise client on options including amendments or appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action: scope and priority
rubrics_metrics.description: An office action represents the government’s official position on the pending patent application and may address almost any aspect of the application; the most important parts touch upon the basic questions related to the patentability of the pending claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inform the client immediately when an office action arrives and explain the patent office’s findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement rejections and rebuttal methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner may question whether the description provides sufficient disclosure for an ordinary person skilled in the art to understand and practice the invention (enablement rejections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebut by showing where the description discloses the allegedly missing subject matter, argue that the missing matter was sufficiently known in the prior art and not necessary for enablement, or amend claims to remove the contested feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner finds even one piece of prior art that reads on one of the claims, they will reject the pending claim as having been anticipated by the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overcome by distinguishing the claims from the cited prior art, arguing examiner misinterpretation, or amending claims to avoid the cited disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (inventive step) rejections and rebuttals
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner finds that a combination of prior art discloses the claimed invention and that a person of ordinary skill would be motivated to combine them, the examiner will reject the claim for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebut by arguing examiner misunderstood cited references, misunderstood the applicant’s invention or claims, arguing lack of motivation to combine, showing secondary indicia, or amending claims to recite nonobvious features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete responses to office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter’s reply must fully answer (respond to) all of the examiner’s comments in the office action; failure to respond to all rejections and points will render the response nonresponsive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most offices impose time limits on responses. A complete response is essential because not responding in full can seriously impair the client’s rights and lead to rejection. If nonresponsive, examiner may reject application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits and extensions for responding to office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most patent offices impose time limits for filing responses; some allow an initial period without fee and an extension period with an extension fee (e.g., typical U.S. office action: three months initial, three additional months with fee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time periods vary widely among offices. Patent drafter must understand country-specific rules and whether time runs from mailing date or office action date. Extensions may be limited or conditional in some countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client involvement and strategic choice over claim amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter should explain draft responses to the client and give the client the opportunity to choose among amendment options, balancing narrower claims overcoming prior art against business objectives and enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clients may know which claim elements are critical to business; narrowing can overcome examiner objections but may make it easier for competitors to design around. Counsel clients on tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new matter in amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: When amending the application, a universal rule in most jurisdictions is that no new matter (new subject matter) beyond that originally disclosed as of the filing date may be added (except to remedy obvious mistakes). The same rule applies to claims, description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all amendments are supported by original disclosure; determine original disclosure carefully when drafting and when preparing amendments to avoid introducing new matter that could invalidate or render amendments inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options to accelerate examination (PPH, accelerated programs)
rubrics_metrics.description: As appropriate, the patent drafter may ask for an accelerated examination if the office offers such a service. The Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) also functions as an accelerated examination scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accelerated examination may require payment of additional fees or meeting specific requirements; PPH relies on favorable results in another office to speed examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand examiners’ practices and prior art standards
rubrics_metrics.description: During substantive examination, examiners compare applicant-cited prior art and their own search results with pending claims. Examiners are typically grouped by technical subject and may repeatedly cite certain favored prior art. Examiners need only find prior art made publicly available before the filing/priority date; they have no duty to find the earliest or best disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that cited prior art may not be the best possible reference; prepare arguments and evidence accordingly and be aware of typical examiner behavior in technical area.
